command:
mkdir -p /workspace/sections && cat > /workspace/sections/1.md <<'EOF'
### 1. Custom sandbox templates

**E2B:** Templates are declared in the SDK (`Template().fromBaseImage()`/`fromTemplate()`, `.copy()`, `.setEnvs()`, `.setStartCmd(cmd, readyCheck)`). Each one is built into a named, tagged template. The start command runs during the build and is captured in a snapshot, so the process is already running when a sandbox starts. Builds are cached and layered, and E2B recommends templates over snapshots for per-customer environments because they start faster. Docs: https://docs.e2b.dev/template/quickstart

**machine-slop today:** Every machine boots the same read-only ext4 root image. Our only workaround is to set up a machine by hand and `snapshot()` it, and that snapshot can't be built from a spec, has no names or tags, and only restores within the same CPU pool.
EOF
wc -w /workspace/sections/1.md

intent: Write the volumes section to /workspace/sections/2.md.
command:
mkdir -p /workspace/sections && cat > /workspace/sections/2.md <<'EOF'
### 2. Persistent volumes shared across machines

**E2B:** [Volumes](https://docs.e2b.dev/volumes) are named storage that lives apart from any sandbox. You can create, list, inspect or destroy them with `Volume.*`, mount them at create time (`volumeMounts: { '/mnt/data': volume }`) and reuse them across sandboxes over time. The SDK can also read and write a volume when no sandbox has it mounted. ([manage](https://docs.e2b.dev/volumes/manage), [mount](https://docs.e2b.dev/volumes/mount); private beta)

**machine-slop today:** Each machine writes to its own 8 GiB scratch disk, which is removed by `destroy()` or idle expiry. Snapshots and forks copy state and never share it. Nothing outlives a machine except a paused machine or a snapshot.

**Ask:** Add `POST /volumes`, a `volumes` field on create, and file access to volumes from the host.
EOF
wc -w /workspace/sections/2.md

intent: Write the code interpreter gap section to /workspace/sections/3.md.
command:
mkdir -p /workspace/sections && cat > /workspace/sections/3.md <<'EOF'
### 3. Stateful code interpreter with rich results

**E2B:** `runCode()` / `run_code()` runs code in a kernel that keeps state, so variables and imports carry over between calls. Code contexts can be created, listed, restarted and removed, each with its own language (Python, JS/TS, R, Java, bash) and cwd, and several can run in parallel. Results come back typed: images, and Matplotlib charts parsed into structured data (type, title, axis labels, elements) for line, bar, scatter, pie and box plots.

**Us:** agentd only runs one-shot processes and streams back base64 stdout and stderr. There is no persistent interpreter session and no structured result or chart output.

Docs: https://docs.e2b.dev/code-interpreting/contexts, https://docs.e2b.dev/code-interpreting/create-charts-visualizations/interactive-charts
EOF
wc -w /workspace/sections/3.md

intent: Combine sections into one issue body and post it to GitHub.
command: cd /workspace && { echo "The three most important things E2B can do that machine-slop can't yet, based on our READMEs and E2B's docs."; echo; cat sections/1.md; echo; cat sections/2.md; echo; cat sections/3.md; } > issue_body.md && wc -w issue_body.md && jq -n --arg t "Gaps vs E2B: custom templates, persistent volumes, code interpreter" --rawfile b issue_body.md '{title:$t, body:$b}' > issue.json && curl -sS -X POST -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" https://api.github.com/repos/rahul-bangre/machine-slop/issues --data @issue.json | jq '{number, html_url, message}'

intent: Build JSON with Python instead of jq and post the issue.
command: cd /workspace && python3 -I -c 'import json,sys; b=open("issue_body.md").read(); json.dump({"title":"Gaps vs E2B: custom templates, persistent volumes, code interpreter","body":b}, open("issue.json","w"))' && curl -sS -X POST -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" https://api.github.com/repos/rahul-bangre/machine-slop/issues --data @issue.json -o resp.json -w '%{http_code}\n' && python3 -I -c 'import json; r=json.load(open("resp.json")); print(r.get("number"), r.get("html_url"), r.get("message"))'
